reading.body:
Nonprofit AI adoption is measured by sector research organizations, not a real-time registry, and the binding constraint is governance capacity rather than compute or power.

The seven sources split the problem into distinct angles. CEP and NTEN survey how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The AI Equity Project tracks access and training gaps. Candid tracks grantmaking for AI adoption and technology infrastructure. Census BTOS includes nonprofit-heavy service sectors in its adoption series, and Stanford HAI reports macro social impact. No single entity maintains a real-time registry.

The practical uses named are grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets. Because governance capacity is the stated constraint, AI scaling in this sector is limited by oversight and policy adoption, not by access to compute or grid power. The data does not support a compute or power constraint for nonprofits.

The data does not provide adoption rates, budget figures, or compute and power requirements. It identifies who publishes sector research, not how many nonprofits have deployed AI or what infrastructure they use.

summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The clearest measured figure for this sector comes from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, which asks firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. For Other services, the NAICS 81 grouping that includes grantmaking and civic organizations, the latest share answering yes is 15.0%, up from 13.7% in the prior period. The series was first asked in September 2023. That is the only hard adoption number in the material, and it covers a broader services grouping rather than nonprofits alone.

On what the sector does with AI, the sources describe activity more than they quantify it. The Center for Effective Philanthropy's sector research, including its AI-focused reporting, examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications. The Nonprofit Technology Network runs regular sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits, and frames its work around equitable use of technology, noting that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector. Candid, the nonprofit data organization behind GuideStar and Foundation Center, tracks grantmaking trends including funding directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure, and its page emphasizes unrestricted support, impact evaluation, and transparency in grantmaking data.

Where organizations and money concentrate is only partly visible here. This site's own catalogue of nonprofits and open source foundations lists four individually verified organizations, two nonprofits and two open source foundations, and states plainly that none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used to benchmark model quality, and the page argues that neutral, open evaluation infrastructure matters because model comparison depends on it while sitting outside the commercial incentives of the labs being evaluated. Khan Academy is described as an end-user of AI capability in education, not a producer of it, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative software that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. The same page notes what is absent: no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations releasing weights for public use, with the notes confirming only organizational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.

On ROI, the harvested material is largely silent. No source here reports a return figure, a cost saving, or a measured productivity gain from AI in nonprofit work. The closest thing to evidence is structural: Candid's page stresses that recognition, media coverage, partnerships, and growth do not guarantee a nonprofit's financial sustainability and that organizations need continued unrestricted support, and it notes that impact evaluations are becoming more important for both nonprofits and funders. Stanford HAI's AI Index, which the sourced points call the citable macro series, describes a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating, and adoption spreading while the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology fall behind, and it notes that data transparency in the field is declining.

On risk and regulation, the material offers posture rather than rules. Stanford HAI says it is collaborating with the founder of the AI and LegTech Lab at The Hague University of Applied Sciences on a project about AI-relevant regulatory frameworks, aimed at improving predictability and legal certainty for providers and users of AI technology through a judicial decision database. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs to make AI accessible, ethical, and practical, turning public libraries and community spaces into learning environments and running a global network that provides standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities. NTEN asks practitioners to pledge to use its Equity Guide and prioritizes equity in technology use, funding, and creation. None of these sources states a compliance obligation specific to nonprofits.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a modest set of conclusions. Adoption in the Census Bureau's broader services grouping sits at 15.0%, so most firms in that grouping are not using AI in any given two-week window, and the sector's own infrastructure organizations are few and mostly not builders. The recurring themes across CEP, NTEN, Candid, and the AI Equity Project are capacity and equity rather than tooling: digital maturity, training gaps, funding for technology infrastructure, and evaluation. The sources do not supply nonprofit-specific ROI evidence or a nonprofit-specific regulatory regime, so a deployment case here would rest on the organization's own capacity and mission fit rather than on numbers these pages provide.

https://cep.org/.brief: The page from the Center for Effective Philanthropy features an article by Kevin Bolduc, who is identified as vice president of assessment and advisory services. The article’s title asks how one collaborative’s movement-led participatory model makes a difference for grantees. The harvested text does not include any further details or findings.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid says it provides comprehensive grants and nonprofit data to help users find funding, research nonprofits, and connect with funders. The page also notes that donors are increasingly using AI tools to research causes and charities. According to the text, this means many donors will never see a nonprofit's website, donation page, or newsletter.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index.brief: The AI Index at Stanford HAI describes its mission as supplying unbiased, globally sourced data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public, tracking and visualising data on the field. This year's edition, the page says, shows a widening gap between what AI can do and our readiness to manage it, with technical capabilities, investment and adoption advancing while governance and evaluation frameworks lag. The page states that previous editions have been cited in newspapers including The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, drawn hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It describes the programme as an independent Stanford HAI initiative led by an interdisciplinary steering committee, and notes a collaboration with Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez on regulatory frameworks.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page catalogues four individually verified organisations classified as nonprofits or open-source foundations, each with a sourced note on governance model and funding, and states that every entry carries the source that decided its classification and the date that source was last read. According to the page, LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a shared evaluation platform used by the wider AI community to benchmark model quality, while Khan Academy is described as an end-user rather than a producer of AI capability in education. The Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation are said to steward creative software tools that AI-generated imagery and 3D content increasingly intersect with, though the page notes their primary missions predate and are not defined by AI. The page states that none of the four are infrastructure builders in the compute-or-power sense, and that the list contains no training compute providers, no standards bodies setting grid or data-center specifications, and no open-model foundations that release weights publicly. It adds that the notes confirm only organisational structure and nonprofit status, not funding scale, compute access, or governance detail.
